title: What If Humans Still Had Tails? You Had One, for About Eight Weeks

scenes.text: What if humans still had tails? You did have one. For about eight weeks.
Every human embryo grows a tail. By the eighth week, most of it is gone, leaving the tailbone: a few fused vertebrae at the base of your spine.
Our ancestors lost the real thing around 25 million years ago, when the ape line split from the monkeys.
In 2024, scientists at NYU found the switch: a jumping gene that landed inside a gene called TBXT and changed how it's read.
They put the same change into mice. The mice were born with short tails, or none at all.
But some of those mice had spines that didn't close properly, like spina bifida. Losing the tail may have cost us. And a few dozen people have been born with one anyway.

description:
What if humans still had tails? Every human embryo grows one, and by about the eighth week most of it has disappeared, leaving the coccyx of fused vertebrae. Tails vanished from our ancestors' fossil record roughly 25 to 20 million years ago, after the ape lineage split from Old World monkeys.
In February 2024, researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine reported in Nature that an AluY jumping gene inserted into the TBXT gene altered its splicing; mice engineered with the change were born with shortened or missing tails, and some showed neural tube defects similar to spina bifida, hinting at a hidden cost. Doctors have recorded about 40 to 59 cases of people born with a tail in modern history.
